role: ESG investment analyst at a mutual fund company
headline: Two years crunching data at a ratings agency, just moved to the investment research department of a mutual fund company in Shanghai's Lujiazui, briefing fund managers on the carbon emissions and governance risks of steel, power and chemicals, and often asked 'will this make money?'
unit: The investment research department of a mid-sized mutual fund company in Lujiazui, Shanghai, with a three-person ESG team serving equities, fixed income and two carbon-neutral thematic funds
education: Master's degree (environmental economics and policy, a one-year program abroad)
level: You can rate an industry on ESG by yourself, read carbon emissions data and sustainability reports, and write due diligence memos. When a fund manager presses you at the investment committee on what it does to valuation, your answers still don't come out cleanly
intro: At the ratings agency you scored thousands of companies, and never once saw a fund manager buy or sell a stock because of your score. Now you sit on the buy side, in the research department, with the steel analyst on your left and a fund manager running billions on your right. As of today, you have to make them believe that carbon emissions and boardrooms are things that belong in the price too.
salary_note: Estimate: an investment research job at a Shanghai mutual fund company, monthly pay plus the year-end bonus spread across the months, runs fifty to seventy percent above the national figure. In bad market years the bonus is halved, and non-core teams like ESG get cut first.

facts.label: Sustainable Investment Analyst (current level)
facts.value: 2-4 years, ¥10,030–14,750 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: Next level up
facts.value: Senior ESG Analyst / ESG Investment Manager (4-7 years)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: On-site due diligence and talking through what needs to improve

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Presenting the ESG view to the investment committee

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 1 related job listing nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: Metro Line 2, packed all the way to Lujiazui. In the elevator you finish the overnight news: a chemical company fined by environmental authorities, a European disclosure rule postponed again.

The research morning meeting. The sector analysts give their views one by one, and when it's your turn you have two minutes on whether the chemical company's fine will affect its environmental approvals and expansion. The fund manager doesn't look up.

You open the data terminal and pull five years of carbon emissions per ton of steel for a steel company, set against its peers. In the third year its figure suddenly falls thirty percent, and you mark a question mark beside it.

The office tower canteen downstairs, a ¥28 set meal. Over lunch you and a colleague from fixed income talk about a green bond, and she asks whether the solar plant listed among its funded projects was ever actually built.

You go through the steel company's sustainability report, a hundred and twenty pages, and find the fine print on the emissions page: the reporting boundary changed, and a subsidiary was carved out. You replace the question mark with a sentence.

The quarterly ESG review of a carbon-neutral thematic fund's holdings. You run the screening rules in Python and two stocks breach them. You write an email to the fund manager, rewording it three times.
A foreign shareholder wants a stewardship report in English. You revise the Chinese draft paragraph by paragraph as the lights come on in the Oriental Pearl Tower outside the window.

Back in your rented flat in an old walk-up, you open a commentary on the international sustainability disclosure standards. Halfway through, the fund manager messages you: that steel company, do you think it's a buy?

ladder.title: ESG Research Assistant
ladder.focus: Collect data, read reports, track policy.

ladder.title: Sustainable Investment Analyst
ladder.focus: Rating models, climate risk analysis, due diligence reports.

ladder.title: Senior ESG Analyst / ESG Investment Manager
ladder.focus: ESG integration strategy, transition finance assessment, engagement with companies.

ladder.title: ESG Fund Manager / Director of Sustainable Investment
ladder.focus: Manage portfolios and set strategic direction.

ai_tasks.name: Presenting the ESG view to the investment committee
ai_tasks.how: AI can summarize research from every side, organize the data and draft the presentation and likely Q&A. A person sets the view and the position, answers challenges in the committee, and answers for the recommendation.

ai_tasks.name: ESG rating and transition risk analysis for a steel company
ai_tasks.how: AI can pull the company's disclosures, emissions data and industry benchmarks, and draft the rating and a list of transition risks. A person judges whether the data can be trusted and whether the transition path is realistic, and gives an opinion with a position on whether to buy.

ai_tasks.name: Reviewing whether a green bond's funded projects comply
ai_tasks.how: AI can compare the funded projects in the offering circular against the green bond catalogue item by item and mark doubtful or mismatched ones. A person only needs to spot-check the borderline cases and sign off.

ai_tasks.name: Updating regulatory tracking and giving internal briefings
ai_tasks.how: AI can monitor new rules, compare old and new provisions, write summaries and produce briefing materials. A person spot-checks that the key clauses are understood correctly, then gives the talk and takes questions.

ai_tasks.name: Building ESG factors into the valuation model
ai_tasks.how: AI can run scenarios, set up the model framework and do sensitivity analysis. A person decides how ESG factors map onto cash flows and discount rates, and explains why those assumptions are reasonable.

ai_tasks.name: On-site due diligence and talking through what needs to improve
ai_tasks.how: AI can help prepare the due diligence checklist and sort through penalty records beforehand. Seeing what's really there, negotiating with management, judging whether they'll really change and building trust all have to be done by a person.

ai_tasks.name: Designing the ESG screening rules for a carbon-neutral thematic fund
ai_tasks.how: AI can compare similar products, test the holdings and sector mix under different screening rules and draft the rule text. A person sets the product's philosophy and the trade-offs, and decides after working it through with the product and compliance departments.

events.e_first_catch: In one company's sustainability report you find emissions reductions that don't match its environmental impact filings. Three months later the company is exposed for environmental problems and its share price drops twenty percent. At the morning meeting the fund manager says one sentence: that was the one you flagged, right?
events.e_ignored: You write a twenty-page transition risk report recommending cutting a coal power company. At the investment committee the fund manager says it has the highest dividend yield this quarter, and your report goes into the appendix.
events.e_report_season: Late April, and thousands of listed companies publish annual reports and sustainability reports all at once. For two weeks you read reports until the small hours every night, Scope 1, Scope 2, Scope 3 swimming in your eyes.
events.e_site_visit: You go with the sector analyst to visit a steel mill in Hebei, standing beside the electric arc furnace in a hard hat as the heat rolls over you. On the high-speed train back you change an assumption in the model: its share of electric furnaces is higher than the report says.
events.e_bonus_cut: The market falls all year, and the company halves the year-end bonus. The ESG team is asked how much it contributes to performance, and the three of you write a very long explanation.
events.e_love: At a sustainable finance forum you meet someone who trades in the carbon market. After the session the two of you walk along the Bund for a long time, talking about nothing but the carbon price.
events.e_greenwash: A company holding a green loan is exposed by the press for describing a coal-fired boiler project as an energy-saving retrofit. Your carbon-neutral fund holds it, and you write an incident note overnight and send it to the client managers first thing in the morning.
events.e_ai_rating: The company buys an AI rating tool: drop in a report and in ten minutes you have a draft rating and a list of controversies. What used to take you a week, you can now get through for a whole industry in a day, and you spend the rest of the time phoning companies.
events.e_vote: At a portfolio company's shareholder meeting there's a resolution to guarantee loans for a party related to the chairman. You write a recommendation to vote against; the fund manager hesitates a day and finally signs against. The resolution passes anyway.
events.e_policy_wave: The stock exchanges issue guidelines on sustainability reporting for listed companies, and a large number of companies must now disclose. Your phone suddenly gets busy: company board secretaries asking how to write it, sales asking if you can build a product.
events.e_wedding: You get married in a very simple ceremony, without a single disposable plate. Both sets of parents find it a bit shabby, and you say it's part of my job.
events.e_cfa: You pass the ESG investing certificate and sign up for CFA Level I. Every evening after work you do practice questions in the café downstairs, and the barista already knows your order.
events.e_house: The two of you buy a small two-bedroom just outside the Outer Ring in Pudong, the down payment emptying both families' savings. On the day you sign you wonder what the embodied carbon of this flat might be, and don't work it out.
events.e_baby: Your child is born. When you come back from leave the team's system has been replaced, and a colleague says AI has already run ratings for your whole industry, waiting for you to review.
events.e_backlash: Abroad there's a wave of anti-ESG sentiment, and several foreign institutions dissolve their teams. The company holds a meeting on whether to fold the ESG team into research. It survives, but you're renamed 'sustainability research'.
events.e_ai_memo: AI can compare a green bond's offering circular against the green catalogue clause by clause and flag doubts, and it writes the first draft of the memo for you too. Your work every day now is judging which of the doubts it flags are real.
events.e_engagement: For a year you talk with a power company's board secretary, urging them to disclose a retirement schedule for their coal units. In this year's annual report, that page finally appears. You save a screenshot of it.
events.e_insomnia: A fund launch, quarterly reports, investment committees and a foreign client's questionnaire all land in the same month. For weeks you can't sleep, still turning over a model assumption at three in the morning.
events.e_parent: Your father goes into hospital back home, and you take a high-speed train through the night. In the ward you join an investment committee on your laptop, holding his hand while you're on mute.
events.e_fund_launch: A transition-themed fund you helped design is launched. The subscriptions on launch day aren't as good as you hoped, but the screening rules you wrote into its prospectus are later copied by several competitors.
events.e_team: The first graduate you hire says at her interview that she chose this field because the river by her childhood home turned black. Three years later she writes, on her own, a report that makes a fund manager change a position.
events.e_eyes: Years of staring at reports and spreadsheets on screen, and your eyes start to go; to read small print you hold the phone further away. You turn the font size on your computer up two notches.

c_valuation.title: Get ESG into the valuation models
c_valuation.situation: Fund managers don't read ratings; they read valuations. You want to put carbon prices, environmental fines and transition capex into the sector analysts' cash flow models, but that means first learning their methods, then persuading them to let you touch their models.

options.label: Learn it, and touch their models
options.result: You spend three months working late with the steel analyst and add carbon costs to his model. The first time at the investment committee the fund manager asks how much each ¥10 rise in the carbon price hits profit, you have the answer.

options.label: Get the ratings solid first
options.result: You feel the ratings themselves aren't good enough yet and leave valuation alone. Your rating reports get more and more detailed, but at the investment committee they still go in the appendix.

c_hk.title: Go to a foreign asset manager in Hong Kong
c_hk.situation: A foreign asset manager's sustainable investment team in Hong Kong is hiring someone who writes Chinese and English and knows mainland listed companies. Thirty percent more pay, half the living space, and a team that headquarters could cut at any time.

options.label: Go to Hong Kong
options.result: You move into a twenty-square-meter flat on Hong Kong Island and write due diligence reports on mainland companies in English every day. The first time headquarters calls your report 'insightful', you laugh out loud in the elevator.

options.label: Stay in Shanghai
options.result: You say mainland companies should be watched from the mainland. The headhunter says let's keep in touch, and you mute her on WeChat.

c_ai_flow.title: Learn to be the reviewer of AI ratings
c_ai_flow.situation: The company wants to roll the AI rating tool out to every industry and needs someone to design the human-machine process: AI drafts, people review what and how, and who signs when there's a mistake. Your boss wants you to lead it, but you also know that once the process is set, the team may not need as many people.

options.label: Lead the process design
options.result: You turn every data trap you've hit over the years into a review rule: boundary changed, subsidiary carved out, figures estimated. After it goes live, the companies your team of three can cover triple.

options.label: Stick to your own industries
options.result: You say you'd rather get to the bottom of steel and power. Someone else sets the process, and the boundary problems the AI misses are still the ones you find, one by one.

c_senior.title: Go for Senior ESG Analyst, and start engaging with companies
c_senior.situation: Your boss says a Senior ESG Analyst will be promoted, to represent the firm in talks with portfolio companies on governance and emissions and to take part in transition finance assessments. You need to produce a report that can change a position, and prove you can hold your own across the table from a listed company's board secretary.

options.label: Go for it
options.result: You pick a power company and write forty pages, from coal retirement to shareholder returns. The fund manager reads it and cuts the position by half, and for the first time you feel your words land on real money.

options.label: Polish for two more years
options.result: You don't feel ready to talk to companies yet and keep writing reports in the background. Your boss says fine, next time.

c_corporate.title: Go do sustainability at an electric car maker
c_corporate.situation: An electric car maker is looking for someone who knows how capital markets read things, to be its sustainability manager: writing the report, dealing with ratings agencies, planning emissions cuts. Twenty percent more pay, and you go from watching others to being watched.

options.label: Go to the corporate side
options.result: For the first time you're on the side being rated, and only now do you learn how many departments one number in a report has to pass through.
options.end: You became head of sustainability at a car maker, writing a thick report every spring, then sitting in a meeting room being questioned point by point by analysts like the one you used to be. You answer patiently.

options.label: Stay on the buy side
options.result: You say you'd still rather be the one asking the questions. The people from the car maker say come back and talk anytime, and you add their report to your tracking list.

c_rating_agency.title: Go back to the ratings agency as head of research
c_rating_agency.situation: The ratings agency where you used to work is setting up a transition finance research center and wants you back to run it, leading ten people on methodology. About the same pay, no more being asked 'can this make money', but you'd also be further from investment decisions.

options.label: Go back and lead the team
options.result: You return to that familiar building, and the first thing you do is change three points in the rating methodology you thought were wrong back then.
options.end: You became head of research at a ratings agency, revising the methodology again and again with a group of young people. Each year a few companies change their disclosures because of your scores, and you think that's enough.

options.label: Stay at the fund company
options.result: You say you still want to stay close to the money and see where it actually flows. Your old colleagues say come back and visit often.

c_head.title: Become Head of Sustainable Investment
c_head.situation: The company is upgrading the ESG team to a sustainable investment department. Its head runs product design, the team and every external position, chases clients with sales, argues clauses with compliance and asks the leadership for budget. Your boss asks if you'll take it.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: You start sitting in budget meetings, interviewing and going on roadshows with sales, your desk covered with prospectuses and team weekly reports. The last time you wrote a due diligence report from scratch yourself was six months ago.

options.label: Stay in research
options.result: You turn it down, saying you still want to do research. The department brings in a head from outside, who asks your opinion before every investment committee.

c_pm.title: Take over an ESG fund as its fund manager
c_pm.situation: The manager of the carbon-neutral thematic fund has left, and the company wants you to take it over, moving from research to running a portfolio. Once you do, every day's net asset value is written after your name, and clients' redemption calls come to you.

options.label: Take the fund
options.result: In your first month in charge the net asset value falls eight percent. You don't change the screening rules, and in the quarterly report you write a long passage explaining why.

options.label: Stay as head of research
options.result: You say you're better suited to seeing things clearly from behind. The new fund manager sits in your office for an hour every week, always asking the same question: has this company really changed, or is it just writing reports?

c_slow.title: Slow down, or keep pushing
c_slow.situation: Several numbers on your checkup are flagged yellow, and your child has started primary school with no one to supervise homework in the evenings. You could ask your boss to cover two fewer industries and stop traveling, and your year-end bonus would shrink.

options.label: Ask to slow down
options.result: You hand over two industries and get home before seven every day. For the first time your child tells you about school, and you listen carefully.

options.label: Keep pushing
options.result: You say these years are the crucial ones. You hire an after-school tutor and watch your child do homework over video every night.

endings.retire: On your last day you take down the row of sustainability reports from the office shelf. The earliest few have yellowed, the emissions in them still calculated by hand. You keep one and put the rest in the recycling bin. As you leave the building, the old buildings across the river light up one after another.
endings.burnout: That spring, reporting season, a fund launch and a big drawdown all pile up together, and as you stand up in a meeting room everything goes black. The doctor orders six months' rest. When you come back the company has you do investor education, explaining what sustainable investing is. You speak slowly, and the people below listen carefully.

stages: You follow a few high-carbon industries on your own. Every day you pull emissions and penalty records from the data terminal, read one company's sustainability report after another, and update ratings and controversies in the firm's ESG database; every week you hand in a brief for the research morning meeting and review the thematic funds' holdings. Whatever a fund manager asks, you have to work it out before you open your mouth.

You start going out to engage on the firm's behalf. Every month you meet board secretaries and sustainability teams at several portfolio companies, arriving with a list of questions and leaving with commitments; at the investment committee your view no longer goes in the appendix, and fund managers press you on valuation impact. In your hands are due diligence memos, voting recommendations and an engagement tracker, and the name signed on them is yours.

You run a department of five or six. In the morning you review the team's ratings and reports, in the afternoon you design screening rules for new funds with the product department and fight over a clause with compliance, in the evening you see institutional clients with sales. You sign off the annual stewardship report and the regulator's questionnaires. You rarely read a report from start to finish yourself now; more of your time goes to setting positions, asking for budget and hiring.

You manage the firm's sustainable investment direction and several funds' portfolios. Every day you watch net asset values and holdings and discuss trades with analysts, and every quarter you write clients a long letter; outside, you speak for the firm at forums, inside, you hold to a long-term judgment against short-term losses at the investment decision meeting. What you say ends up in other people's research reports.
work: A fixed income colleague brings a green bond's offering circular and asks whether its funded projects comply. You compare it against the green catalogue clause by clause all afternoon, and beside the fourth project you write: suggest asking whether it's new build or retrofit.

A chemical company's board secretary replies to your email that emissions data can't be broken down by product. You dig out the unit-level data they filed in their environmental impact assessment and politely attach it.
You clean up coal capacity and utilization hours for thirty power companies in Python and plot a scatter chart. The sector analyst looks at it and says, I want to use that chart.

You spend an afternoon with a cement company's management as they explain their alternative fuels plan. You keep asking where the money comes from and which year it goes in, and in the end they agree to publish a timetable at their next results briefing.
Proxy season: in one week you review over forty resolutions, and on a director pay plan you write against, with three lines of reasons. The fund manager asks if that's enough, and you say it is.

The bank's transition finance team asks whether the targets on a sustainability-linked loan are reasonable. You lay out that steel mill's last five years of data and say it would hit this emissions target without changing anything.

The product department brings a draft of screening rules for a new fund. You go through it line by line in the meeting room and strike two of them, saying those two exist only to make the holdings look greener.
You interview ten graduates. The one you keep got a question wrong, but was the only one who asked you 'where does this data come from?'
The regulator sends a questionnaire on sustainable investing, thirty-odd pages. You and two others work on it for a week, and before submitting you check that every 'yes' has evidence behind it.

A portfolio company is hit by a workplace safety accident. Before the market opens you call the team into the meeting room, and in twenty minutes it's decided: cut the position by half, and send the company a letter of inquiry.
A pension client comes to ask why your fund has lagged its benchmark for three years. For two hours you lay out every stock you didn't buy and why, and in the end they renew.

An analyst brings you an AI-written company deep dive and says the argument is very clear. You read it and ask one question: the emissions path it describes, where does the money come from? The analyst goes back and rewrites it for a week.
past: You go to middle school in Xiangtan, Hunan, near an old steel works. You remember the winter sky being gray, and laundry hung outside collecting a film of black soot.

In the gaokao (college entrance exam) you get into economics at a university in Shanghai. When filling in your choices you thought about environmental engineering, but your father said economics would make money.

In your third year you take an environmental economics elective, and in the lecture on carbon pricing you feel for the first time that the gray you saw as a child is something that can be put into a price.

You go abroad for a one-year master's in environmental economics and policy, writing your thesis on the abatement costs of China's steel industry. To pay the tuition, your family sells a flat back home.

Back in China you join an ESG ratings agency as a research assistant, reading over a hundred reports a day and keying figures into the database. After a year you know on which page companies like to hide their numbers.
An older schoolmate at a fund company says they're building an ESG team and asks if you'd come to the buy side. You say yes; you want to see whether anyone actually uses those scores.

late.pension_note: Estimate: thirty-odd years of contributions to Shanghai's basic pension for company employees at the maximum contribution base, plus the company annuity, comes to roughly thirty to forty percent of your final monthly pay, not counting bonuses.
scenes: For the first few months of retirement you still open the news in the morning to see which company has been fined. Then, with no brief to write, you put down the phone and go to the market.
A university asks you to teach a course on sustainable finance. The first assignment you give the students is to find the most deeply buried number in a sustainability report.
You go back to Xiangtan. The old steel works is a park now, with one chimney left standing. You take a photo beneath it and send it to the fund manager who brought you up.
Your grandchild asks what you used to do. You say you helped people see whether companies were clean. He asks what clean means; you think for a long time, and say it means not lying.
You don't watch net asset values anymore, and walk a lap of the park every morning. Sometimes, walking, a number from some report comes back to you, and you shake your head and keep going.
An analyst you trained calls to say a company's data looks too good. You ask her only one thing: has the reporting boundary changed? She says she'll check.
When the time comes you retire. You leave your investor education slides to whoever takes over; the last slide says: first look at where the data comes from.
In the first year away from the research department, whenever you wake at the time of the morning meeting, you catch yourself thinking about what you'll say in your two minutes today.
You find your footing in the new role. Running into that fund manager at a forum now and then, he says you were right about that coal power company, just three years early.
The graduate you hired later becomes head of sustainable investment at a fund company. In an interview she says her first teacher taught her to ask where the data comes from.

Later mandatory disclosure becomes normal, and AI can read a whole report in a second. But which numbers are true and which promises will be kept, someone still has to go sit across the table and ask.
One winter you notice the sky outside your window is much bluer than when you were a child. You don't know whether any of that is yours; you just stand on the balcony a little longer.

closing.retire: Many years later, walking along the Huangpu, you watch an electric ferry come across from the far bank, almost silent. You remember the line you once wrote in a report, 'transition takes a long time', and stand there until it docks.
closing.burnout: Many years later you find on your bookshelf that twenty-page coal power transition risk report, printed out, your notes in the margins. You leaf through a few pages and put it back where it was.
closing.end: One spring many years later, reporting season comes round again, and on the news you see thousands of companies publish their reports at once. You don't open any of them; you just push the window open and let the wind in.
